It is designed for relatively simple projects with limited assembly requirements. Not every PCB assembly project qualifies for this offer. Your project must meet the technical requirements listed below, and the promotion is subject to customer eligibility and usage limits. $29 PCB Assembly Requirements To qualify for the $29 PCB assembly offer, your project must meet all of the following requirements: Component Sourcing: All components must be supplied by PCBWay. PCB Type: Only rigid PCBs are eligible. Flex PCBs and rigid-flex PCBs are not supported by this offer. Assembly Quantity: No more than 20 boards per order. Components per Board: Each board can have a maximum of 200 components. Total Component Quantity: The total number of components across the order cannot exceed 600. Unique Component Types: The project can include no more than 100 different component types. Through-Hole Solder Joints: The total number of through-hole solder joints cannot exceed 100. All limits are inclusive. For example, an order for exactly 20 boards or a project with exactly 100 different component types can qualify, provided that all other requirements are also met. Important: Meeting these technical requirements does not automatically guarantee the promotional price. Your order must also meet the applicable customer eligibility and monthly usage limits. How Often Can You Use the $29 PCB Assembly Offer? The $29 PCB assembly promotion has a monthly usage limit based on customer status. New customers: Eligible new customers can use the offer once per month. Returning customers: Eligible returning customers can use the offer up to twice per month. If you submit multiple orders at the same time, only one eligible order can receive the $29 promotional price. The remaining orders will be charged at their applicable rates. Please note that each order must meet all the technical requirements to qualify for the promotion. The monthly usage limit does not mean that every order you submit will receive the special price. How to Get $29 PCB Assembly on PCBWay Follow these steps to get started. Step 1: Prepare your PCB design files Prepare your Gerber files, Bill of Materials (BOM), and pick-and-place file, as applicable to your project. Step 2: Check your project requirements Confirm that your project uses rigid PCBs, that all components will be supplied by PCBWay, and that your assembly quantity and component counts are within the specified limits. Step 3: Submit your assembly order Visit the PCBWay PCB Assembly Service page and submit your PCB assembly files and requirements. Step 4: Confirm your eligibility Check your eligibility for the promotion and make sure you have not exceeded the applicable usage limit. The final price is subject to order review and confirmation. Frequently Asked Questions -Can I use the $29 PCB assembly offer for flex PCBs or rigid-flex PCBs? No. The promotion is available for rigid PCBs only. Flex PCBs and rigid-flex PCBs are excluded. -Can I supply my own components? No. All components must be supplied by PCBWay to qualify for this offer. -Can I order more than 20 boards? No. The maximum eligible assembly quantity is 20 boards per order. -How many components can my PCB have? Each board can have no more than 200 components, and the total component quantity across the order cannot exceed 600. -Is there a limit on component types? Yes. The project can include no more than 100 different component types. -Are through-hole components allowed? Projects with through-hole components may qualify, provided that the total number of through-hole solder joints does not exceed 100 and all other requirements are met. -Can I apply the $29 price to multiple orders submitted at once? No. Only one eligible order can receive the promotional price when multiple orders are submitted together. -Can I use the offer again next month? The promotion may be available again according to the applicable monthly usage limit. Please check your eligibility before placing another order. -Does the $29 price cover my entire PCB project? The $29 offer is a special PCB assembly price, not necessarily the total cost of your project. PCB fabrication, components, shipping, and other applicable charges may be quoted separately. Verify Now Blog > Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips by: Mila Sep 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout analog vs digital circuits analog and digital circuits analog circuits digital circuits mixed signal PCB design We often say that the world of chips consists of only 0s and 1s. But more accurately, digital circuits use defined voltage ranges to represent discrete logic states, while the real world is clearly not like that. Human voices have different volumes, light has different levels of brightness, temperature changes continuously, and radio waves do not simply jump between 0 V and 1 V. So here is the question: If CPUs mainly process digital data, how can a smartphone hear sound, capture photos, connect to a cellular network, and charge its battery? The answer lies in three types of chips: digital chips, analog chips, and mixed-signal chips. Understanding the differences between them is also important for PCB layout , because digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits have different requirements for signal integrity, grounding, power, and noise control. （class B analog audio amplifier） Analog vs Digital Circuits: What Is the Difference? The key difference between analog vs digital circuits is how they represent and process signals. Digital signals focus on discrete states. In a typical digital circuit, voltage is divided into high and low ranges, which are interpreted as 1 and 0. As long as the signal remains within the specified range, small amounts of noise usually do not change the logic result. Analog signals, on the other hand, preserve continuous changes. The small voltage generated by a microphone, the radio-frequency signal received by an antenna, changes in temperature detected by a sensor, and the voltage and current during battery charging and discharging can all vary continuously over time and amplitude. A simple way to understand analog and digital circuits is: A digital signal is like written text. It mainly cares about which character is being represented. An analog signal is like speech. It contains not only information, but also volume, tone, speed, and many subtle changes. In other words, digital circuits are good at processing discrete information, while analog circuits directly interact with continuously changing signals from the real world. （Analog vs Digital Signals） Digital Chips: Computing, Control, and Memory Digital chips are best suited to problems that can be clearly defined and represented as discrete data. Common digital chips include: CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs; MCUs and various controllers; DRAM, SRAM, and NAND Flash; FPGAs; Digital interface and network processing chips. Digital circuits are built from large numbers of logic gates, flip-flops, registers, and memory cells. Driven by a clock, data flows and is processed according to defined rules. Their biggest advantage is their high level of abstraction. Engineers can move from transistors to logic gates, then to adders, processors, instructions, and software. This allows complex systems to be designed, verified, and optimized at different levels of abstraction. Digital chips are particularly suitable for: Executing programs; Storing data; Implementing complex control functions; Performing large-scale logic and mathematical operations; Precisely coordinating different functions within a system. However, digital circuits themselves cannot directly process continuously changing analog signals. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. The process can be simplified as: Real world → Analog signal → ADC → Digital data → Digital processing → DAC → Analog signal → Real world For example, during audio recording and playback, a microphone first converts sound into an analog electrical signal. The analog front end processes the signal, and an ADC converts it into digital data. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. A mixed-signal chip is not simply a combination of an ADC and a DAC. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? A smartphone is a typical example of a system that combines all three types of chips. It needs to process digital data while constantly interacting with the analog signals of the real world. When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Digital circuits are built from large numbers of logic gates, flip-flops, registers, and memory cells. Driven by a clock, data flows and is processed according to defined rules. Their biggest advantage is their high level of abstraction. Engineers can move from transistors to logic gates, then to adders, processors, instructions, and software. This allows complex systems to be designed, verified, and optimized at different levels of abstraction. Digital chips are particularly suitable for: Executing programs; Storing data; Implementing complex control functions; Performing large-scale logic and mathematical operations; Precisely coordinating different functions within a system. However, digital circuits themselves cannot directly process continuously changing analog signals. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. The process can be simplified as: Real world → Analog signal → ADC → Digital data → Digital processing → DAC → Analog signal → Real world For example, during audio recording and playback, a microphone first converts sound into an analog electrical signal. The analog front end processes the signal, and an ADC converts it into digital data. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. A mixed-signal chip is not simply a combination of an ADC and a DAC. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? A smartphone is a typical example of a system that combines all three types of chips. It needs to process digital data while constantly interacting with the analog signals of the real world. When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Design a Ground Guard Trace in PCB Design How to Design a Ground Guard Trace in PCB Design by: Mila Oct 20,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout In PCB design , a ground guard trace is a copper trace connected to ground and placed alongside a signal trace or around a sensitive circuit area. It can help reduce unwanted capacitive coupling and electromagnetic interference (EMI) in certain applications. However, a ground guard trace is not a universal solution. Its effectiveness depends on the signal type, operating frequency, grounding structure, and return-current path. This article explains how a ground guard trace works, when to use a PCB ground guard, how to design one, and which common mistakes to avoid. What Is a Ground Guard Trace? A ground guard trace is a grounded copper trace placed alongside a signal trace or around a sensitive circuit area to help reduce unwanted electromagnetic coupling. Depending on the layout, related structures may include ground rings and ground via fences. These structures serve different purposes. A ground guard trace runs alongside a signal or sensitive node, a ground ring surrounds a specific circuit area, and a ground via fence uses a row of grounded vias to create a more continuous shielding structure along a PCB boundary or signal route. A properly designed ground guard trace can help intercept electric-field coupling and provide a path for some unwanted currents. However, its performance depends on its connection to the ground plane, the surrounding geometry, and the signal's return path. Ground guarding should be considered one of several PCB grounding techniques, not a replacement for a well-designed stackup, continuous reference planes, or proper signal routing. Which PCB Signals Need a Ground Guard Trace? Not every signal benefits from a ground guard trace. The decision should be based on signal sensitivity, operating frequency, potential noise sources, and the available return path. Signal or Circuit TypeIs a Ground Guard Trace Recommended?Design ConsiderationsCrystal oscillators and clock circuitsMay be beneficialConsider the oscillator topology, parasitic capacitance, grounding, and manufacturer's layout recommendations.High-impedance analog signalsOften worth evaluatingA guard trace may help reduce capacitive coupling and leakage effects when properly designed.High-speed differential pairsNot automaticallyMaintain pair symmetry and controlled impedance. Additional ground traces may affect impedance and coupling.DDR and other high-speed busesUsually not applied indiscriminatelyPrioritize routing rules, continuous reference planes, and signal integrity.Low-speed control signalsUsually unnecessaryAdequate spacing and good routing are often sufficient.Power tracesDepends on the circuitPrioritize current capacity, voltage drop, thermal performance, and return-current paths.Signals routed near the PCB edgeMay be beneficialA grounded via fence or suitable grounding structure may help improve isolation. The key is to identify the actual interference mechanism before adding a guard structure. In many cases, improving the return path or increasing spacing is more effective than adding a ground guard trace. When Should You Use a Ground Guard Trace? Crystal Oscillators and Clock Circuits Crystal oscillator circuits and clock signals can be sensitive to parasitic capacitance, unwanted coupling, and layout variations. A suitable grounded structure may help isolate the circuit from nearby noise sources. However, placing a ground guard trace too close to an oscillator or its signal nodes can increase parasitic capacitance and affect oscillation performance. Follow the oscillator manufacturer's layout recommendations and verify the design when necessary. For high-speed clock traces, prioritize a continuous reference plane, controlled routing, and a short return-current path. Add a ground guard trace only when it provides a clear benefit. Precision Analog and High-Impedance Signals High-impedance analog nodes, sensor inputs, and sensitive amplifier circuits may be affected by capacitive coupling or leakage currents. In these cases, a ground guard trace can help reduce coupling from nearby signals. For particularly high-impedance circuits, a driven guard may be more appropriate than a grounded guard, depending on the circuit topology. These approaches are not interchangeable and should be evaluated against the circuit's electrical requirements. Keep the guard structure close enough to provide useful isolation, but ensure it does not introduce excessive parasitic capacitance. Clean layout practices, suitable materials, and proper grounding are also important. Areas With Potential Return-Path Discontinuities A signal's return current generally follows the path of lowest impedance, often concentrated beneath the signal trace on its reference plane at high frequencies. If a signal crosses a gap or split in its reference plane, the return current may be forced to detour. This can increase loop inductance, degrade signal integrity, and increase electromagnetic emissions. The preferred solution is to route the signal over a continuous reference plane or redesign the layer arrangement. If a transition between reference planes is necessary, provide an appropriate return-current path. For example, a ground stitching via may help when the reference planes are connected to the same ground network. A ground guard trace cannot compensate for a fundamentally discontinuous reference plane. Fix the return path first, then evaluate whether additional guarding is necessary. Signals Routed Near the PCB Edge Signals routed close to a PCB edge may have stronger electromagnetic coupling to their surroundings, depending on the geometry and operating frequency. A grounded via fence may help contain fields or improve isolation in some designs. Its effectiveness depends on via spacing, connection to the reference plane, and the electrical characteristics of the signal. Do not assume that every edge-routed signal requires a ground guard trace or via fence. Evaluate the actual layout and its EMI requirements. Sensitive Signals Near Strong Noise Sources When sensitive analog or control signals must be routed near switching regulators, high-speed digital interfaces, or other potential noise sources, a ground guard trace may provide an additional layer of isolation. However, increasing the physical separation between noisy and sensitive circuits is often the better first step. Keep switching-current loops compact, place components appropriately, and avoid routing sensitive signals through noisy regions whenever possible. Use ground guarding as a supplementary measure when basic placement and routing improvements are insufficient. When Should You Avoid a Ground Guard Trace? Ordinary Low-Speed Digital Signals Most low-speed digital signals do not require dedicated ground guard traces. Adequate spacing, sensible routing, and a continuous reference plane are generally sufficient. Adding unnecessary guard traces consumes routing space and can complicate the layout without providing a measurable improvement. Power Traces and High-Current Paths Power traces should be designed primarily around current capacity, voltage drop, temperature rise, and return-current behavior. A ground trace placed beside a power trace does not automatically improve power integrity or reduce noise. For switching power supplies, prioritize compact high-current loops, appropriate component placement, and well-designed input and output paths. High-Speed Differential Pairs Without Verification Differential pairs rely on controlled geometry and electromagnetic coupling between the two conductors. Adding a grounded trace beside a pair may change its impedance, field distribution, and coupling characteristics. For USB, Ethernet, PCIe, and other high-speed interfaces, follow the applicable routing and impedance requirements. Do not add ground guard traces unless the design has been evaluated through appropriate calculations, simulation, or measurement. Short Connections Between Nearby Components Short connections between adjacent components often do not benefit from dedicated ground guard traces, especially when the circuit already has a good reference plane and sufficient spacing. Instead of adding unnecessary copper, focus on minimizing connection length, maintaining a clear return path, and avoiding interference from nearby noise sources. Common PCB Ground Guard Mistakes Even a properly intended ground guard trace can cause problems if it is poorly designed or incorrectly connected. The following table summarizes common PCB ground guard mistakes, their potential effects, and ways to avoid them. Ground Guard Trace Design Guidelines Effective ground guarding requires more than simply placing a grounded trace beside a signal. Consider the following factors during PCB design. Determine the Appropriate Spacing The spacing between the signal and guard trace affects parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic coupling. The optimal distance depends on the signal's electrical requirements and the surrounding geometry. Do not treat rules such as 3W spacing as universal ground-guarding requirements. Such rules are layout guidelines, not guarantees of a specific level of isolation. Use impedance calculations or electromagnetic simulation when the design is sensitive to small geometry changes. Connect Ground Structures Properly A ground guard trace should connect to an appropriate ground network. For longer guard structures, ground via stitching may help maintain a low-impedance connection to the reference plane. Via spacing should be selected according to the operating frequency, the desired level of isolation, the PCB stackup, and manufacturing constraints. A fixed spacing such as 0.5–1 mm is not suitable for every design. For critical applications, verify the via-fence structure using electromagnetic simulation or measurement. （Ground Guard Trace and Ground Via Stitching） Choose a Suitable Trace Width The guard trace width affects its electrical behavior, manufacturing feasibility, and the space available for signal routing. Select a width that meets fabrication requirements and works with the intended grounding structure. Wider traces do not necessarily provide better shielding in every situation. Their benefit depends on the overall geometry and electrical connection. Maintain a Continuous Return Path A continuous reference plane is often more important than adding a ground guard trace. Make sure the signal has a suitable return-current path throughout its route, including at layer transitions and near changes in reference-plane geometry. When a signal changes layers, consider the relationship between its reference planes and whether an appropriate ground stitching via is needed nearby. Preserve Differential-Pair Geometry For high-speed differential signals, maintain the required differential impedance, spacing, and symmetry. Any added ground structure should be evaluated as part of the complete transmission-line geometry. Do not assume that surrounding a differential pair with grounded copper will automatically improve signal integrity or reduce EMI. Keep Noisy and Sensitive Circuits Properly Separated Ground guarding works best as part of a broader PCB layout strategy. Separate sensitive analog circuitry from switching nodes and high-current paths where practical, minimize high-frequency current loops, and provide appropriate decoupling. A well-designed stackup and grounding system should come first. Additional guard structures should address a specific, identified interference problem. Practical Examples of PCB Ground Guarding The following examples illustrate situations in which a ground guard trace or related grounding structure may be worth evaluating. They are design scenarios rather than guaranteed performance results; the actual improvement depends on the PCB layout and should be verified. Example 1: Reducing Coupling Into a High-Impedance Sensor Input A sensor input with a high source impedance is routed near a digital signal. Capacitive coupling from the digital trace may introduce unwanted noise into the measurement. One possible approach is to increase the spacing between the two traces and, if necessary, add a properly grounded guard trace around the sensitive input. The design should then be evaluated by measuring the input noise or comparing simulation results. Example 2: Improving Isolation Near a PCB Edge A signal routed close to the edge of a PCB may require additional isolation to meet an EMI target. A grounded via fence may be considered along the relevant edge or boundary. The via geometry and connection to the reference plane should be designed for the signal's operating frequency. Compare emissions or coupling before and after the change to determine whether the structure provides a measurable benefit. Example 3: Addressing Interference Near a Switching Regulator A sensitive analog trace is routed near a switching regulator. Before adding a ground guard trace, inspect the switching-current loop, component placement, reference plane, and distance between the noisy and sensitive circuits. If these fundamentals are already well designed, a grounded guard may be evaluated as an additional measure. The final layout should be validated through testing or simulation rather than relying on the presence of a guard trace alone. Conclusion A ground guard trace can help reduce unwanted coupling in selected applications, including high-impedance analog circuits, sensitive signal routes, and certain EMI-sensitive areas. However, its effectiveness depends on the grounding structure, signal geometry, operating frequency, and return-current path. For reliable PCB design , start with a suitable stackup, continuous reference planes, correct routing, and effective separation between noisy and sensitive circuits. Then use a PCB ground guard, ground ring, or ground via fence where analysis shows that it can provide additional benefits. For critical designs, verify the results through simulation and measurement rather than relying on fixed rules or assumptions. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. However, pin names alone do not tell the whole story. Always check the IC datasheet to confirm each pin’s function and recommended connections. During PCB layout , pay particular attention to switching nodes, feedback paths, and grounding. Proper component placement and routing can help reduce noise, improve power integrity, and ensure stable operation. Whether you’re designing a simple power supply or a more complex DC-DC converter, understanding these pins is an important step toward reliable PCB design.
